svg.title: The weight and feeding-tube window: three tubes, each given its own slot by the guidelines
svg.desc: Schematic of the weight and feeding-tube decision window plus where each tube enters the body. The top timeline has four phases: diagnosis to pre-treatment assessment, 5–6 weeks of chemoradiotherapy, (trimodality) waiting and surgery, and after surgery at home; a schematic weight curve declines slowly and a horizontal line marks 'minus 10%' as the threshold for starting assessment and dietitian input (ESPEN wording), not an order to place a tube. Annotations: 17% had lost more than 10% in the 3 months before diagnosis (Rotterdam surgical cohort, n=922), with 5-year mortality HR 1.34 and no increase in complications; losing more than 5% during chemotherapy gave postoperative infectious complications OR 2.69 (OGSG1003, SCC, n=134); 80% of neoadjuvant patients had dysphagia, 48% got a tube and 27.9% of those hardly used it (n=127); cachexia after chemoradiotherapy 60.7%, and a pre-treatment stoma helped only when the tumour filled 70% or more of the lumen (NCKU, n=260). Four tube bars: nasogastric tube for expected enteral nutrition under 4 weeks (ESGE 2021); gastrostomy (PEG) for over 4 weeks, gastric route first (ESGE), with no effect on later gastric-conduit reconstruction (meta-analysis, n=1,027); feeding jejunostomy considered intraoperatively in major upper-GI surgery (ESPEN surgery Rec 23, Grade B), with ESGE reserving the jejunal route for an unusable or poorly emptying stomach or high aspiration risk; a metal stent drawn dashed and crossed out — ESGE 2021 does not recommend it as a bridge to surgery or before chemoradiotherapy, and in Mariette 2015's matched analysis R0 was 71.0% vs 85.5% and 3-year overall survival 25% vs 44%. The lower half shows a side-view figure: the nasogastric tube runs from the nose through the oesophagus into the stomach; the PEG enters the stomach through the abdominal wall; the jejunostomy enters the jejunum through the abdominal wall. Three pros-and-cons boxes: the nasogastric tube needs no anaesthesia, can be removed any time, dislodges more often, interferes less with swallowing and is weaned earlier after radiotherapy; PEG is placed endoscopically, by the introducer technique in stenosis, with meta-analysis showing no difference in leak, stricture, complications or stay, 1 of 96 PEG-site biopsies malignant, fewer dislodgements and possibly better quality of life; the jejunostomy is placed laparoscopically or at open surgery, with bowel obstruction about 6% (over 63% reoperated), site infection 7%, malfunction 7%, no proven benefit from routine placement, and home feeding for 6 weeks after surgery reducing more-than-5% weight loss from 82% to 28% (n=41).

g.text: WEIGHT × FEEDING ROUTE × TIME
The weight and feeding-tube window: three tubes, each given its
own slot by the guidelines
Top: the timeline — losing a tenth of body weight is the threshold for starting an assessment, not an order to place a tube;
each of the three tubes has its own time-point and precondition in the guidelines. Bottom: where each enters the body.
None is 'best'; a stent is not the answer before chemoradiotherapy.
Weight (schematic)
−10%: the threshold to start assessment and dietitian input (ESPEN wording)
Diagnosis → pre-treatment assessment
Chemoradiotherapy, 5–6 weeks
(Trimodality) wait and surgery
After surgery, home
Nasogastric tube
Expected enteral nutrition <4 weeks (ESGE 2021); named with PEG in the ESPEN radiotherapy section
Gastrostomy (PEG)
Expected >4 weeks: consider a percutaneous tube, gastric route first (ESGE 2021); PEG did not compromise later gastric-conduit reconstruction (meta-analysis,
Feeding jejunostomy
Considered intraoperatively in major upper-GI surgery (ESPEN surgery Rec 23, Grade B); ESGE: jejunal route only if the stomach is unusable, empties poorly or
aspiration risk is high
Metal stent
ESGE 2021: not recommended as a bridge to surgery or before chemoradiotherapy (strong). Mariette 2015 matched: R0 71.0% vs 85.5%, 3-year OS 25% vs 44%
Lost >10% in the 3 months before diagnosis: 17% (Rotterdam surgical cohort, n=922) → 5-year mortality HR 1.34; complications not increased
Lost >5% during chemotherapy → postoperative infectious complications OR 2.69 (OGSG1003, SCC, n=134)
80% of neoadjuvant patients had dysphagia, 48% got a tube, 27.9% of those hardly used it (n=127)
Cachexia after chemoradiotherapy 60.7%; a pre-treatment stoma helped only when the tumour filled ≥70% of the lumen (NCKU, n=260)
Nasogastric tube
Gastrostomy (PEG)
Jejunostomy
Stomach
Oesophagus
Jejunum
Diaphragm
Nasogastric tube
Medical: no anaesthesia, fastest to place, removable any
time; dislodges more often than PEG (ESPEN);
misplacement into the airway needs a verification
protocol (ESGE)
Practical: less dysphagia and earlier weaning after
radiotherapy (ESPEN); visible on the face
Gastrostomy (PEG)
Medical: placed endoscopically; the introducer (push)
technique avoids pulling through the tumour in
oesophageal stenosis (ESGE); meta-analysis of 4
retrospective studies, n=1,027: no difference in leak,
stricture, complications or stay, no PEG-site leak (Fang
2022); 1 of 96 PEG-site biopsies malignant (Bhatti 2015)
Practical: fewer dislodgements, possibly better quality
of life (ESPEN); under the clothes
Feeding jejunostomy
Medical: placed laparoscopically or at open surgery, usually intraoperatively; meta-analysis (Shen 2021): bowel obstruction ~
6% (>63% of those reoperated), site infection 7%, malfunction 7%; routine placement not shown beneficial (Mei 2021)
Practical: home feeding can continue for 6 weeks after surgery (small RCT, n=41: >5% weight loss 28% vs 82%)
Whether placing a tube first improves outcomes cuts both ways in retrospective data (two US surgical cohorts saw no benefit; NCKU saw it only when the tumour filled ≥70% of the
lumen) — 'who should get one first' is closer to the real question than 'whether'. NHI: enteral formula code 05101B lists oesophageal cancer; the PEG code 33108B neither names nor
excludes it, and stent code 47058B being reimbursed does not mean it is recommended — ask the billing office or case manager.
Schematic, redrawn from the ESPEN 2021 practical guidelines on cancer and surgical nutrition, the ESGE 2021 enteral-tube guideline (parts 1 and 2), the ESGE
2021 oesophageal stenting guideline, van der Schaaf 2014, Aoyama 2023 (OGSG1003), Huerter 2016, Chiang 2026, Fang 2022, Bhatti 2015, Shen 2021, Mei 2021,
Mariette 2015 and Baker 2015 | cohorts, designs and endpoints differ — numbers are not directly comparable; the choice of tube is the team's, for your situation
